name: Plan-Making Effect
summary: Making a specific plan for an unfinished goal stops it from intruding on your thoughts, even though you have not reached the goal yet.
explanation:
The plan-making effect is the finding that an unfinished goal stops nagging you once you make a concrete plan for it. E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister described it in 2011, in a paper titled "Consider it done!".

Earlier research on the Zeigarnik effect showed that unfinished tasks stay active in memory and intrude on unrelated work. Masicampo and Baumeister reproduced that: participants with an unfulfilled goal had more intrusive thoughts and did worse on an unrelated task. But when participants made a specific plan (what they would do, when and where), the intrusions and the drop in performance disappeared. The goal still wasn't done. The plan alone was enough to tell the mind that it could stop monitoring it.

This is why capture-and-clarify systems work. In Getting Things Done, once you write down an open loop and decide its next action, you can stop thinking about it. There is a condition, though: the plan has to be specific, and you have to trust that you will follow it. A vague "I'll deal with it later" does NOT close the loop. The same mechanism is behind the ready-to-resume plan, a short note you write before an interruption to reduce attention residue.

Keep in mind that the original studies were small lab experiments with students. The direction of the effect fits a large body of goal research, but the exact size in daily life is uncertain.

articles.title: Consider It Done! Plan Making Can Eliminate the Cognitive Effects of Unfulfilled Goals
